extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (metaphysics, epistemology) interested in perception, identity over time, and causation
extracted.subtask_description: A close conceptual analysis of the notions used in the philosophy of physics and mind: what counts as a physical thing/persistent matter, the role of continuity and dynamics in identity over time, the status of sense-data (illusions, dreams, hallucinations), and a critical examination of the 'law of causality'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Physical things
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical things are those series of appearances whose matter obeys the laws of physics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay down the following definition: physical things are series of appearances whose matter obeys the laws of physics. Such series exist empirically, and this existence constitutes the verifiability of physics. The text notes we may assume uniqueness of grouping of appearances so that the resulting things obey physical laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity as first characteristic of identity over time
rubrics_metrics.description: Two appearances of the same piece of matter at different times must be connected by a series of intermediaries; the appearances must permit a hypothetical complement of 'sensibilia' preserving continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity is largely hypothetical (we do not observe things continuously); during uninterrupted observation it is nearly verified but can fail in rapid motions (explosions). We may admit unobserved 'sensibilia' required to preserve continuity when forming identity judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity is necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity alone does not guarantee material identity; in many slowly changing cases it suffices, but in approximately homogeneous fluids it fails utterly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: one can travel by sensibly continuous gradations from any one drop of the sea at one time to any other drop at another time, so continuity cannot distinguish pieces of matter in such cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity with the laws of dynamics as additional criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to continuity, conformity with dynamical laws is required to regard appearances at different times as the same piece of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting from common-sense persistent things and making reasonable modifications yields assemblages of 'sensibilia' that obey certain simple laws (dynamics). We therefore group appearances so that the resulting things obey the laws of physics; this grouping defines motion and material identity practically/theoretically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness assumption for grouping appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: For unambiguous identity, there should be only one way of grouping appearances so that the resulting things obey the laws of physics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text admits difficulty in proving uniqueness, but for present purposes assumes only one grouping yields series that obey physics; this assumption underpins definitional treatment of physical persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of matter may be secured by definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The persistence of all matter throughout time can (in principle) be secured by definition once we adopt the above grouping criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests that given the empirical fact of series obeying physics, one can define persistence accordingly; further elaboration (invoking a thing's history) can reduce reliance on unperceived 'sensibilia'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense-data in dreams/hallucinations are 'given' like waking data
rubrics_metrics.description: Dream-objects and hallucinations are as much given to the subject as waking sense-data; they occupy positions in the private space of the subject's perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dream-objects fail in correlation with other private spaces and with perspective space, but in the sense in which 'there' can be a datum, they are 'there' just as truly as waking sense-data. The difference lies in their lack of continuity and correlation with past/future and others' experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: data vs inferred 'things' (existence/reality predicates apply to descriptions, not data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Predicates like 'real', 'unreal', 'exists', 'does not exist' apply meaningfully to propositions or descriptions, not to immediate sense-data (names). It is therefore meaningless to ask whether a datum 'exists'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the theory of descriptions: 'existence' is applicable only to descriptions; use examples (Homer, God) to show how proper names are used as descriptions. Thus 'My present sense-datum exists' is meaningful, but saying of a datum x 'x exists' is strictly meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusions/unreality stem from inference errors, not from status of data
rubrics_metrics.description: Abnormal sense-data regarded as deceptive have the same ontological status as other sense-data; they differ in their correlations/causal connections with other 'sensibilia' and 'things'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because usual correlations become part of unreflective expectations, we mistakenly call unusual cases 'unreal' whereas they are causes of false inferences. The unusual correlations are (the author thinks) physically or physiologically explicable and raise complications but no philosophical objection to realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of deceptive appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: Deceptive/unreal appearances fall into different classes requiring different treatment: (a) variety of normal appearances across perspectives, (b) unusual cross-sense correlations (e.g., bent stick), (c) dreams lacking continuity/correlation, (d) hallucinations detectable only via discrepancy with others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each class is addressed: (a) different perspectives are explained by multiple perspectives model; (b) cross-sense discrepancies are false inferences not illusions; (c) dreams condemned for lack of continuity/correlation with waking data; (d) recurrent hallucinations (e.g., insanity) cannot be decided theoretically by patient vs friends' mendacity—no internal criterion exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event must be a universal (repeatable) for causality claims
rubrics_metrics.description: In statements of causal laws, an 'event' is intended not as a particular whole state of the universe but as a universal (a repeatable, sufficiently broadly defined kind of occurrence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defined too narrowly (including force, exact temperature, etc.), an event will occur at most once and the law becomes trivial; events should be broad enough to admit many particular occurrences, e.g., 'striking a match' rather than specifying every condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal characterization of the law of causality (criticized)
rubrics_metrics.description: One plausible formulation: Given any event e1 there is an event e2 and a time-interval τ such that whenever e1 occurs, e2 follows after an interval τ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is elicited from dictionary/philosopher definitions and is used to expose problems (e.g., specification of τ, what counts as 'whenever', problems of environmental interference during τ). The author does not accept this as the scientific practice's guiding principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal contiguity of cause and effect is impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: Cause and effect cannot be strictly contiguous in time because the time-series is compact (no two instants are contiguous); therefore there must be a finite interval τ separating cause and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If contiguity is insisted upon, a dilemma arises: causes lasting in time either require causal relations among their parts (leading to infinite regress) or be static and then curiously 'explode' into effects without prior change. Thus contiguity is rejected and a finite τ is assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of 'same cause same effect' formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim 'same cause, same effect' is otiose because when antecedents are specified sufficiently fully to compute consequents, they become so complex that recurrence is unlikely; science therefore does not rest on invariant uniformities of this crude kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As sciences advance they replace crude regularities by more differentiated antecedents; including more of the environment reduces probability of exact recurrence. The observed regularities are useful heuristics in early stages but are not strict postulates of physics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events/causes need not resemble their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim that 'cause and effect must resemble each other' is misplaced; in legitimate senses of 'cause' and 'effect', they are often very dissimilar—cause is typically a state of the whole universe, effect a particular event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This undermines arguments that certain phenomena (e.g., mind arising from matter) are impossible because of dissimilarity between cause and effect; legitimate scientific laws allow wide dissimilarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of analogy between causation and volition (nexus fallacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is mistaken to suppose that cause is analogous to volition requiring an intelligible 'nexus' between cause and effect; laws used in physics leave no room for such nexus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers who demand an 'intelligible' link between cause and effect are importing a psychological analogy which is not warranted by the formal laws that replace causality in physical science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsion and determination are not intrinsic to causation
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that a cause 'compels' or 'determines' an effect (in a sense where effect cannot determine cause) is misleading; 'compulsion' presupposes thwarted desire and is irrelevant where desire doesn't enter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an agent does what he desires, there is no compulsion even if his actions are predictable from antecedents. Thus invoking notions of compulsion or special determination misconstrues scientific regularities and their relation to human volition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of 'necessity' in causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessity must be understood as a predicate of propositional functions (true for all values of an argument); to apply 'necessary' to a proposition one must fix which constituent is being varied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'If x is a man, x is mortal' is necessary when x is the argument variable. Applied to causality, the relevant variable is the time of occurrence of the earlier event; so causal regularities are intended to be necessity with respect to occurrence time, yielding formulations like 'for any time t1, if e1 occurs then e2 occurs after τ'.
